sections.title: Introduction to Systems Thinking — What is a System?

blocks.html: Start here Kill all the snakes in a forest because “snakes are bad”. Soon there are too many rats, the rats eat all the grass, and the forest suffers. One small change, one big mess. Systems thinking teaches you to ask “What else will this affect?” before you act.
blocks.text:
Start here Kill all the snakes in a forest because
“snakes are bad”. Soon there are too many rats, the rats eat all the
grass, and the forest suffers. One small change, one big mess. Systems
thinking teaches you to ask “What else will this
affect?” before you act.

blocks.html: This week is taught by Prof. Shiva Subramaniam, with Prof. Prasanna, Prof. Sivakumar, Lt Col Jayakumar and Prof. Kartic sharing habits.

blocks.html: Why learn it? We often feel upset because we don’t understand why things happen, or why people behave the way they do. Systems thinking helps you understand the world. Prof. Shiva says the TCS leader F. C. Kohli told him in 1993 to learn it. He ignored that advice for years, and now regrets it.
blocks.text:
Why learn it? We often feel upset because we don’t understand why things happen, or why people
behave the way they do. Systems thinking helps you understand the world. Prof. Shiva says the TCS leader F. C. Kohli told him in 1993 to learn it. He ignored
that advice for years, and now regrets it.
The definition

blocks.html: A system is an interconnected set of elements that is coherently organised in a way that achieves something (a purpose).
blocks.text:
A system is an interconnected set
of elements that is coherently organised in a way that achieves
something (a purpose).

blocks.html: Every system has three parts:
blocks.text: Every system has three parts:

blocks.caption:
Elements, interconnections, and a
function or purpose.

blocks.html:
Part Meaning Example: the digestive system
Elements The parts Mouth, tongue, oesophagus, stomach, liver, intestines…
Interconnections How the parts link and depend on each other Food passes from the mouth to the stomach to the intestines
Function / purpose What the system achieves To digest food
blocks.text: Part Meaning Example: the digestive system Elements The parts Mouth, tongue, oesophagus, stomach, liver, intestines… Interconnections How the parts link and depend on each other Food passes from the mouth to the stomach to the intestines Function / purpose What the system achieves To digest food

blocks.html: Systems inside systems: the human body has the digestive, nervous and circulatory systems. Each one interacts with the others to keep you alive.
blocks.text:
Systems inside systems: the human body has the
digestive, nervous and circulatory systems. Each one interacts
with the others to keep you alive.
A heap vs a system

blocks.caption:
Remove a stone from a heap and nothing
happens. Remove a wall from a house and it falls.

blocks.html:
Heap (not a system) House (a system)
A pile of 100 stones Walls, doors, windows, roof, foundation, all connected
Remove one stone: still a heap, just 99 stones Remove the foundation or a wall: the house collapses
Not affected when one part is removed Affected when one element is removed
blocks.text: Heap (not a system) House (a system) A pile of 100 stones Walls, doors, windows, roof, foundation, all connected Remove one stone: still a heap, just 99 stones Remove the foundation or a wall: the house collapses Not affected when one part is removed Affected when one element is removed

blocks.html: Easy test: If removing one part changes the whole thing, it’s a system.
blocks.text:
Easy test: If removing one part changes the whole
thing, it’s a system .
What is systems thinking?

blocks.html:
Systems thinking is a holistic approach to understanding:

  1. how the elements of a system are connected to each other,
  2. how the system relates to larger systems, and
  3. how a change in one part affects the rest.
blocks.text:
Systems thinking is a holistic
approach to understanding: how the elements of a system are connected to each other, how the system relates to larger systems , and how a change in one part affects the rest .

blocks.html: Lecture example — the food chain In a jungle, the hawk, snake, bird, grasshopper, grass, mouse, owl, rabbit and fox are all connected. Remove the snakes, and the rats multiply and destroy the grass. Animals that depend on the grass suffer too. One missing element affects the whole system. Many climate problems happen because we remove elements without asking, “What will happen if I do this?”
blocks.text:
Lecture example — the food chain In a jungle, the
hawk, snake, bird, grasshopper, grass, mouse, owl, rabbit and fox are
all connected. Remove the snakes , and the rats multiply
and destroy the grass. Animals that depend on the grass suffer too. One
missing element affects the whole system. Many climate
problems happen because we remove elements without asking,
“What will happen if I do this?”

blocks.caption:
Everything in the food chain is connected.
Remove one link and the whole chain is affected.

blocks.text: What can you use it for?

blocks.html:
• Examining problems in your family, campus or life
  • Understanding situations and people
  • Diagnosing what is really wrong
blocks.text:
Examining problems in your family, campus or
life Understanding situations and people Diagnosing what is really wrong

blocks.html: Lecture example — the doctor Even for a headache, a good doctor checks your blood pressure and weight, and asks about your sleep, food and exercise. Why? Everything is connected: Less walking → higher blood sugar → higher blood pressure → faster heart rate → more anxiety → even higher blood pressure. So the doctor treats the whole system, not just one part.

The six blind men and the
elephant

blocks.alt: The blind men and the elephant
blocks.caption:
Each person touches one part
and guesses wrong. Only the whole view shows the elephant.

Tail A rope or snake
Body A wall
Ear A fan
Leg A pillar or tree
Trunk A snake
Tusk A spear

blocks.html: Lesson: The whole is not just the sum of its parts. In life, we often see only one small part and jump to conclusions. Look at how the parts connect before you decide.

sections.title: Examples of a System and the Systems View

blocks.html: Start here Your masala dosa arrives 20 minutes late, and you’re annoyed. But behind that one dosa are a delivery rider, petrol pumps, a restaurant, a supply chain, farmers, the monsoon and the government. Once you see the system, you get less angry.

blocks.html: Lecture example — when fans disappeared During the pandemic, many matches (and the IPL) were played without fans. Several teams said they didn’t perform as well. Prof. Shiva has seen home crowds turn a 2–1 loss into a 3–2 win. Fans are an element too. Remove them, and the system behaves differently.

Example 3: one dosa, many
systems

blocks.caption:
One delivered dosa depends on a
long chain of connected systems.

blocks.html: You ← delivery rider (scooter → petrol → petrol pumps) ← restaurant (chef, cooks, stock) ← supply chain ← food production (rice, dal) ← farmer ← monsoon rain, fertiliser, government support and distribution.

blocks.html: If any one link is affected, your dosa is late. “So many things have to come together for one dosa to reach your house.”

If any one link is affected, your dosa is late. “So many

The systems view

blocks.html: Everything is connected. All things in nature and in the human world exist in one interconnected web of resources, energy, information and relationships. No problem or solution exists in a silo.
blocks.text:
Everything is connected. All things in nature and in
the human world exist in one interconnected web of
resources, energy, information and relationships. No problem or
solution exists in a silo.

blocks.html: So if you have a problem, several systems are causing it. To solve it, find which part of the system is really causing it.
blocks.text:
So if you have a problem, several systems are causing it. To solve
it, find which part of the system is really causing
it.

Video 1: How wolves change
rivers

blocks.html: Lecture example — wolves in Yellowstone When wolves were brought back to Yellowstone National Park (USA) in 1995, they hunted deer and kept them away from some valleys. Without deer over-grazing, trees and plants grew back. With more plants, riverbanks became stronger, so the rivers changed course. One small change, a few packs of wolves, changed the shape of the land.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — wolves in Yellowstone When wolves were brought back to Yellowstone National Park
(USA) in 1995, they hunted deer and kept them away from some valleys.
Without deer over-grazing, trees and plants grew back .
With more plants, riverbanks became stronger, so the rivers
changed course . One small change, a few packs of
wolves, changed the shape of the land.

blocks.caption:
Wolves → fewer deer → more trees →
stronger riverbanks → rivers change.

sections.title: Becoming a Systems Thinker — The Big Picture and Consequences

blocks.html: Start here You failed an exam and feel your life is over. Your friend takes you up in a helicopter. From 2,000 feet, you see your whole life: graduating at 22, a good job at 28, a family, a home for your parents, travelling the world. The exam is still important, but now it’s just one small dot.
blocks.text:
Start here You failed an exam and feel your life is
over. Your friend takes you up in a helicopter . From
2,000 feet, you see your whole life: graduating at 22, a good job at 28,
a family, a home for your parents, travelling the world. The exam is
still important, but now it’s just one small dot.

The 14 habits of a systems
thinker

blocks.html: The Waters Center for Systems Thinking lists 14 habits of a systems thinker. This week’s teachers explain several of them (see the full list on the guidelines page). This page covers two: seeing the big picture and considering consequences.
blocks.text:
The Waters Center for Systems Thinking lists 14 habits of a systems thinker . This week’s teachers
explain several of them (see the full list on the guidelines page). This
page covers two: seeing the big picture and considering consequences .

Habit: Seek to
understand the big picture

blocks.caption:
Go up in the helicopter to see the big
picture, without losing the details.

blocks.html: A big-picture person sees both the narrow picture (the details) and the big picture. Both matter.
blocks.text:
A big-picture person sees both the narrow
picture (the details) and the big
picture . Both matter.

blocks.html: Questions to ask:
blocks.text: Questions to ask:

blocks.html:
• How can I see the big picture without losing sight of important details?
  • How can I widen the boundaries of my system?
    • In space: “I’m not just in the mechanical department. I’m connected to the whole campus.”
    • In time: “Where will I be in 2, 5, 10 years?”
  • How much time should I spend understanding the larger system?
  • Focus on what you can influence, not on what you can’t.
blocks.text:
How can I see the big picture without losing sight of
important details ? How can I widen the boundaries of my system? In space: “I’m not just in the mechanical
department. I’m connected to the whole campus.” In time: “Where will I be in 2, 5, 10 years?” How much time should I spend understanding the larger system? Focus on what you can influence , not on what you
can’t.

blocks.html: Lecture example — the band A drummer in a marching band only hears his own beat. He can’t tell that someone five rows away missed a beat. A person watching from the stands sees both: the drummer doing well, and the one who slipped.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — the band A drummer in a marching
band only hears his own beat. He can’t tell that someone five rows away
missed a beat. A person watching from the stands sees
both: the drummer doing well, and the one who slipped.

blocks.html: Lecture example — rainwater harvesting (Prof. Kartic) In the 1990s, Chennai flats were short of water. It was easy to blame the government. But the big picture was different: the city got enough rain for everyone, and most of it was being lost as run-off into drains. So rainwater harvesting was promoted, and later made compulsory. Each building could do this within its own control, and well water improved quickly.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — rainwater harvesting
(Prof. Kartic) In the 1990s, Chennai flats were short of water.
It was easy to blame the government. But the big
picture was different: the city got enough
rain for everyone, and most of it was being lost as
run-off into drains. So rainwater harvesting was promoted, and
later made compulsory. Each building could do this within its
own control , and well water improved quickly.

blocks.html: Tip: Keep your “helicopter” parked outside your house. Whenever you’re stuck in the narrow picture, go up and look.
blocks.text:
Tip: Keep your “helicopter” parked outside your
house. Whenever you’re stuck in the narrow picture, go up and look.

Habit:
Consider short-term, long-term and unintended consequences

blocks.html: Every action, or non-action, has consequences:
blocks.text: Every action, or non-action, has consequences:

blocks.html:
Type Meaning Prof. Shiva’s sugar example
Short-term What happens right away Blood sugar goes up
Long-term What happens later Kidneys may get damaged
Unintended Side effects you didn’t plan, good or bad Can’t work → can’t earn → can’t buy things you want
blocks.text: Type Meaning Prof. Shiva’s sugar example Short-term What happens right away Blood sugar goes up Long-term What happens later Kidneys may get damaged Unintended Side effects you didn’t plan, good or bad Can’t work → can’t earn → can’t buy things you want

blocks.html: Unintended consequences can be positive too. You help an elderly person cross the road, and that kindness comes back to you in a way you never expected.
blocks.text:
Unintended consequences can be positive too. You
help an elderly person cross the road, and that kindness comes back to
you in a way you never expected.

blocks.html: Questions to ask:
blocks.text: Questions to ask:

blocks.html:
• What are the unintended consequences of this action? What trade-offs should I consider?
  • Can I accept short-term pain for long-term gain?
blocks.text:
What are the unintended consequences of this action? What trade-offs should I consider? Can I accept short-term pain for long-term
gain ?

blocks.html:
Lecture example — Operation Cat Drop (the “Cats in Borneo” video) In the 1950s, DDT was sprayed in Borneo to kill malaria mosquitoes. It worked, but:

  • Lizards (geckos) ate the poisoned insects, and cats ate the lizards. Many cats died.
  • With fewer cats, rats multiplied and brought the risk of disease (typhus and plague).
  • So cats were parachuted into villages: “Operation Cat Drop”. One “simple” fix caused a chain of unintended consequences.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — Operation Cat Drop (the “Cats in Borneo”
video) In the 1950s, DDT was sprayed in Borneo
to kill malaria mosquitoes. It worked, but: Lizards (geckos) ate the poisoned insects, and cats ate the lizards. Many cats died. With fewer cats, rats multiplied and brought the
risk of disease (typhus and plague). So cats were parachuted into villages:
“ Operation Cat Drop ”. One “simple” fix caused a chain
of unintended consequences.

blocks.caption:
DDT → poisoned lizards → cats die → rats
multiply → cats dropped in by parachute.

blocks.html:
Lecture example — outbound training at IIT Madras (Lt Col Jayakumar)

  • Short-term: students hated waking up at 5:30 a.m.; a few twisted ankles.
  • Long-term: students from different departments became friends, gained confidence, and learned to speak in front of 40 people.
  • Unintended: small injuries. Overall, it is remembered fondly.
blocks.text:

blocks.html: Lecture example — “no hands, no legs, no tooth!” A boy learning to cycle shows off: “No hands!”, then “No legs!” — and then he falls. “No tooth!” Short-term: a new skill. Long-term: he knows how to cycle. Unintended: a broken tooth.

sections.title: Mental Models, and How Structure Generates Behaviour

blocks.html: Start here You want to eat fewer snacks. But your snack jars are transparent and sit right where you walk past ten times a day. You keep eating. Is it a lack of willpower, or is it the structure you built?
blocks.text:
Start here You want to eat fewer snacks. But your
snack jars are transparent and sit right where you walk past ten times a
day. You keep eating. Is it a lack of willpower, or is it the structure you built?

Habit:
Consider how mental models affect current reality and the future

blocks.html: Mental models are the pictures and beliefs we build in our minds from what we sense and experience. When something triggers them (a word, an image, a person, an event), they play back automatically.
blocks.text:
Mental models are the pictures and beliefs we build
in our minds from what we sense and experience. When something triggers
them (a word, an image, a person, an event), they play
back automatically.

blocks.html: Mental models shape:
blocks.text: Mental models shape:

blocks.html:
• how we react to things,
  • our thinking and emotional patterns,
  • how we solve problems and handle obstacles,
  • how we manage conflict, and how we make decisions.
blocks.text: how we react to things, our thinking and emotional patterns , how we solve problems and handle obstacles , how we manage conflict , and how we make decisions .

blocks.html: They also influence other people’s mental models, and the other way round.
blocks.text:
They also influence other people’s mental models,
and the other way round.

blocks.caption:
The lens you look through
decides what you see.

blocks.html: Lecture example — the single parent who “couldn’t be promoted” (Prof. Prasanna) A single mother couldn’t travel for work because she cared for her child and elderly parents. Over time she came to believe: “Because I can’t travel, management doesn’t take me seriously.” In coaching, they questioned this: what assumptions and interpretations was it based on? What conclusions had she jumped to without full evidence? Much of it turned out to be her own perception. She replaced that model with one built on the value she could create. Instead of asking managers “What can you offer me?”, she went in saying, “Here’s what our group achieved, and here’s our roadmap.” The managers listened and supported her. It also freed up her mind space, energy and time.

Habit:
Recognise that a system’s structure generates its behaviour

sections.title: Don't Rush, Find the Leverage, Make Connections

blocks.html: Start here In the middle of a seminar, the projector suddenly dies, but the fans and lights still work. Everyone waits for an electrician. One professor, who knows how the hall’s wiring works, simply plugs the projector into another socket. The talk goes on. That’s a leverage point.
blocks.text:
Start here In the middle of a seminar, the projector
suddenly dies, but the fans and lights still work. Everyone waits for an
electrician. One professor, who knows how the hall’s wiring works,
simply plugs the projector into another socket. The talk goes on. That’s
a leverage point .

blocks.html: Prof. Sivakumar explains three habits.
blocks.text: Prof. Sivakumar explains three habits.

Habit
1: Consider an issue fully; don’t jump to a quick conclusion

blocks.html:
• Weigh the options and possible outcomes before you decide.
  • Hasty decisions lead to poor results.
  • The tension while a problem is unsolved is what pushes us into hasty decisions. Accept the tension; don’t let it rush you.
  • Once you decide, communicate it clearly.
  • Sometimes a quick fix is truly needed. That’s fine, but it should be rare.
blocks.text:
Weigh the options and possible outcomes before you
decide. Hasty decisions lead to poor results . The tension while a problem is unsolved is what
pushes us into hasty decisions. Accept the tension; don’t let it rush
you. Once you decide, communicate it clearly . Sometimes a quick fix is truly needed. That’s fine,
but it should be rare.

blocks.html: Lecture example — the student who wanted a new supervisor A research student asked to change his supervisor. After hearing his story, Prof. Sivakumar almost agreed. Then he stopped: “I’ve only heard one side.” He spoke to the supervisor, took time to think, and then held a meeting with both, where the student showed his work so far. The real problem was poor communication: the supervisor had assumed the student wasn’t working. Once they talked, it was solved, without changing supervisors.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — the student who wanted a new
supervisor A research student asked to change his supervisor.
After hearing his story, Prof. Sivakumar almost agreed. Then he stopped:
“I’ve only heard one side .” He spoke to the supervisor,
took time to think, and then held a meeting with both ,
where the student showed his work so far. The real problem was poor communication : the supervisor had assumed the
student wasn’t working. Once they talked, it was solved, without
changing supervisors.

Habit
2: Use the system’s structure to find leverage points

blocks.html: A lever lets a small push lift a heavy load. A leverage point is a place in a system where a small change gives a big result. To find one, you must understand how the system is built.
blocks.text:
A lever lets a small push lift a heavy load. A leverage point is a place in a system where a small change gives a big result . To
find one, you must understand how the system is
built .

blocks.caption:
A small action at the right point gives a
big result.

blocks.html: Lecture example — the projector and the three-phase power The hall had a three-phase power supply, and only one phase had failed. A colleague who knew this plugged the projector into a socket on a working phase. The meeting went on with almost no break. Understanding the structure showed him the leverage point.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — the projector and the three-phase
power The hall had a three-phase power supply,
and only one phase had failed. A colleague who knew this plugged the
projector into a socket on a working phase . The meeting
went on with almost no break. Understanding the structure showed
him the leverage point.

blocks.html: Lecture example — the Leisure Time Activities Programme (LTAP) As Dean of Students, Prof. Sivakumar wanted IIT students to develop all-round, not just academically. After years of exam preparation, many had dropped hobbies. The team did a “time audit”: they mapped a typical student’s 24 hours (classes, mess timings, hostel life, sleep, weekends) to find the free time. They noticed students like a formal structure, like a course. So they created structured programmes (fine arts, literary and cultural skills, personal growth) at the right times, with easy fees and easy payment. It is still running today.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — the Leisure Time Activities Programme
(LTAP) As Dean of Students, Prof. Sivakumar wanted IIT students
to develop all-round, not just academically. After years of exam
preparation, many had dropped hobbies. The team did a “time

blocks.html: Questions to find leverage points:
blocks.text: Questions to find leverage points:

blocks.html:
• What works well in the system? What gives poor results?
  • What does the system achieve overall (the big picture)?
  • What small changes would improve the results a lot?
  • How can the good results last a long time?
blocks.text:
What works well in the system? What gives poor results? What does the system achieve overall (the big
picture)? What small changes would improve the results a
lot? How can the good results last a long time?

Habit
3: Make meaningful connections within and between systems

blocks.html: A system is a set of connected parts. If an important connection breaks, the system can collapse into a heap. So:
blocks.text:
A system is a set of connected parts. If an important connection
breaks, the system can collapse into a heap . So:

blocks.html:
• Spot the connections within a system and between different systems. They can be logical, functional, or cause-and-effect connections.
  • Practise by drawing cause-and-effect diagrams of systems around you. With practice, you begin to see connections that aren’t obvious at first.
blocks.text:
Spot the connections within a system and between
different systems. They can be logical, functional, or cause-and-effect
connections. Practise by drawing cause-and-effect
diagrams of systems around you. With practice, you begin to see
connections that aren’t obvious at first.

blocks.html: Lecture example — the plant Seed → plant → flower → fruit → seed. But the plant is also connected to bees and butterflies (pollination), birds (spreading seeds), sun, water and wind, and even to pests and bad weather. A farmer must understand all these connections to protect the crop and get good seeds.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — the plant Seed → plant → flower →
fruit → seed. But the plant is also connected to bees and
butterflies (pollination), birds (spreading
seeds), sun, water and wind , and even to pests
and bad weather . A farmer must understand all
these connections to protect the crop and get good seeds.

blocks.html: Transfer what you learn: if you understand the leverage points of one system, check whether a similar system has similar ones. This leads to innovation.
blocks.text:
Transfer what you learn: if you understand the
leverage points of one system, check whether a similar
system has similar ones. This leads to innovation .

blocks.html: Learning is about connections too: sun, water and soil help a seed grow; a teacher, books and a good learning space help a mind grow. We learn by observing others (thanks to “mirror neurons”), which builds better relationships and more happiness.

sections.title: Loops, Time Delays, Accumulations and Change Over Time

blocks.html: Start here You’re hungry, so you eat. A few hours later you’re hungry again. Cause and effect often run in circles, not straight lines. And sometimes the effect shows up much later than the cause.
blocks.text:
Start here You’re hungry, so you eat. A few hours
later you’re hungry again. Cause and effect often run in circles , not straight lines. And sometimes the effect
shows up much later than the cause.

Habit:
See the circular nature of cause and effect (feedback loops)

blocks.html: In many systems, A causes B, and B in turn affects A. This is a feedback loop.
blocks.text: In many systems, A causes B, and B in turn affects A. This is a feedback loop .

blocks.caption:
Cause and effect often go round in a
circle.

blocks.html:
Example The loop
Hunger Hungry → eat → full → hungry again
Prof. Shiva’s health (page 1) Less walking → higher sugar → higher BP → anxiety → higher BP
Rumours in an office A draft policy leaks → whispers spread → people react → leaders sense the reaction → the decision is shaped
blocks.text:
Example The loop Hunger Hungry → eat → full → hungry again Prof. Shiva’s health (page 1) Less walking → higher sugar → higher BP → anxiety → higher BP Rumours in an office A draft policy leaks → whispers spread → people react → leaders
sense the reaction → the decision is shaped

blocks.html: Lecture example — the king in disguise Old kings would dress as common people and sit at tea shops to hear what people said about an idea. They used that feedback before taking the final decision.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — the king in disguise Old kings
would dress as common people and sit at tea shops to hear what people
said about an idea. They used that feedback before
taking the final decision.

blocks.html: Lecture example — words shape actions A child hangs from a bar. One passer-by says, “Very good, hold on tight!” Another says, “Don’t — you’ll fall!” The brain grabs the word “fall”, and a fall becomes more likely. “Great minds discuss ideas, average minds discuss events, small minds discuss people.” What we think becomes what we say, and what we say becomes what we do.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — words shape actions A child hangs
from a bar. One passer-by says, “Very good, hold on tight!” Another
says, “Don’t — you’ll fall!” The brain grabs the word “fall”, and a fall
becomes more likely. “Great minds discuss ideas, average minds
discuss events, small minds discuss people.” What we think becomes what we say , and what we
say becomes what we do .

blocks.html: Technology also evolves through loops of feedback and improvement. Radio went from a big box on the wall to a phone app; cameras went from 36-photo film rolls to instant digital photos.
blocks.text:
Technology also evolves through loops of feedback and improvement.
Radio went from a big box on the wall to a phone app; cameras went from
36-photo film rolls to instant digital photos.

Habit: Recognise the
impact of time delays

blocks.html: Cause and effect are often far apart in time. A systems thinker:
blocks.text:
Cause and effect are often far apart in time. A
systems thinker:

blocks.html:
• understands how long the “gestation period” will be before results show, and
  • tells people about the delay, so they don’t get anxious.
blocks.text:
understands how long the “gestation period” will be
before results show, and tells people about the delay, so they don’t get
anxious.

blocks.html: Lecture example — the new education policy It wasn’t brought in overnight. Between the announcement and the final policy, the public gave suggestions, committees and experts discussed them, and social media was full of debate. That delay helped shape a better policy.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — the new education policy It wasn’t
brought in overnight. Between the announcement and the final policy, the
public gave suggestions, committees and experts discussed them, and
social media was full of debate. That delay helped shape a
better policy.

blocks.html: Everyday example: you start exercising today, but you see results only after weeks. Expect the delay; don’t quit after day 3.
blocks.text:
Everyday example: you start exercising today, but
you see results only after weeks. Expect the delay; don’t quit after day
3.

Habit:
Pay attention to accumulations and their rates of change

blocks.html: Some things build up (accumulate) or run down over time. Notice what is accumulating and how fast.
blocks.text:
Some things build up (accumulate) or run
down over time. Notice what is accumulating
and how fast .

blocks.html:
Example What accumulates
Elections Candidates try to build up supporters and votes, from national politics to housing-society elections
Factory inventory Some items move fast and run out; others pile up as dead stock. Both are unhealthy. Just-in-time stock control prevents unwanted build-up.
blocks.text:
Example What accumulates Elections Candidates try to build up supporters and votes, from national
politics to housing-society elections Factory inventory Some items move fast and run out; others pile up as dead
stock . Both are unhealthy. Just-in-time stock
control prevents unwanted build-up.

Habit:
Observe how elements change over time (patterns and trends)

blocks.html:
Lecture example — rainwater harvesting, 20 years later (Prof. Kartic) The 1990s system worked well. But over 20 years:

  • Cars increased, so the soil around the building was paved over and less rain soaked in.
  • More concrete houses were built nearby, and more washing machines meant more waste water.
  • The groundwater became salty, and the city drains began to overflow. Lesson: a one-time fix isn’t enough. Systems change, so keep monitoring and revising, and help everyone understand the bigger system.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — rainwater harvesting, 20 years later
(Prof. Kartic) The 1990s system worked well. But over 20
years: Cars increased, so the soil around the building was paved
over and less rain soaked in. More concrete houses were built nearby, and more washing machines
meant more waste water. The groundwater became salty , and the city drains
began to overflow . Lesson: a one-time
fix isn’t enough. Systems change, so keep monitoring and
revising , and help everyone understand the bigger system.

Habits:
Test assumptions, and check results by “successive approximation”

blocks.html: Ask “What if…?”: Who else will be affected? What else would change? Try something, observe, adjust, and try again.
blocks.text:
Ask “What if…?” : Who else will be affected? What
else would change? Try something, observe , adjust , and try again.

blocks.html: Lecture example — work from home after COVID (Prof. Kartic) Before COVID: long commutes; offices far from the city; companies needed to be near talent. During COVID: everyone worked from home, and companies and employees adapted. After COVID: no commute and lower office costs, but weaker team bonding and harder monitoring. Companies are now testing options: “What if people come to office twice a week?” “What if we rent workstations near employees’ homes?” They observe, fine-tune and try again. The likely result is a hybrid model.

Systems, examples, the systems view and
the habits of a systems thinker.

blocks.text: What is a system?

blocks.html:
• System = elements + interconnections + purpose (digestive system: organs + links + digesting food).
  • Heap vs system: remove a stone from a heap and nothing changes; remove a wall from a house and it falls.
  • Systems thinking = a holistic approach: how parts connect, how a system relates to larger systems, and how one change affects the rest.
  • Food chain: kill the snakes, rats multiply, the grass dies.
  • Doctor: treats the whole body because everything is connected.
  • Blind men and the elephant: the whole is not the sum of its parts.

Examples and the systems
view

blocks.html:
• IIT Madras (students, faculty, facilities; linked to government, parents, alumni).
  • Cricket match (fans are an element too).
  • Food delivery (rider → restaurant → supply chain → farmer → monsoon).
  • Systems view: everything is connected; no problem exists in a silo.
  • Wolves in Yellowstone changed the rivers. We are part of the system too (hot shower, traffic jam).

Habits of a
systems thinker (lecture examples)

blocks.html:
Habit Example
Big picture Helicopter view of your life; the band; rainwater harvesting
Consequences (short, long, unintended) Sugar → kidneys → work; Operation Cat Drop; outbound training; “no tooth!”
Mental models Single parent’s promotion belief; “I’m not creative”
Structure → behaviour Table vs side-by-side; snack jars; WhatsApp routine; sweet shop on the way home
Don’t rush to a conclusion Student’s supervisor change: hear both sides
Leverage points Projector on another phase; LTAP time audit
Connections Plant ↔︎ bees, birds, sun, water; draw cause-and-effect diagrams
Feedback loops Hunger cycle; office rumours; the king in disguise
Time delays Education policy consultation
Accumulations Votes; inventory, dead stock, just-in-time
Change over time Rainwater system 20 years later
Test assumptions Hybrid work: “What if 2 days in office?”

blocks.text: Guidelines

blocks.html:
• 14 habits (Waters Center). Master one every 15 days.
  • Ask: Beyond the problem? Others’ views? Long run? Unintended effects?
  • Books: The Fifth Discipline (Peter Senge); Thinking in Systems (Donella Meadows).
